rules: The handover renders on FIRST ENCOUNTER, not on a fixed tile. introduced_on is an authoring preference for where the copy reads best, never a rule the renderer obeys.
Handed-over state persists against the HOUSEHOLD, not the browser session.
The affordance (dotted underline + popover) renders on every marked term, always, regardless of handover state. A handover shown twice is mildly redundant; one never shown strands someone.
The popover shows glossary then why. Never the handover sentence.
One first-introduction per block, asserted. The renderer never decides what to mark; only <term id> wrappers in the copy do.

equity.handover: This is what everyone means by your equity.
equity.glossary: The part of a property you own outright. Its value, less whatever is still owing on it.
equity.why: It's the figure a lender starts from when you ask them for anything.

lvr.plain: How much of the place is borrowed
lvr.handover: Lenders and brokers call this your LVR, for loan to value ratio.
lvr.glossary: What you still owe, as a share of what the property is worth.
lvr.why: Lenders change the terms they'll offer at certain levels of it, including whether lenders mortgage insurance comes into it.

offset.handover: The account doing that is called an offset.
offset.glossary: An everyday account linked to your loan. Whatever sits in it comes off the balance interest is charged on, and you can still spend it any time.
offset.why: It's the one loan feature that works without you doing anything, and the one most often left half-used.

redraw.plain: Money you've paid ahead and could pull back out
redraw.glossary: Extra repayments you've made that the lender may let you take back. Unlike an offset, the money is theirs to control and the terms can change.
redraw.why: It looks like savings on a statement and behaves differently when you need it.

variable_fixed.handover: A rate that can move is called variable. One that's locked for a period is fixed.
variable_fixed.glossary: Variable rates move when the lender moves them. Fixed rates stay put for an agreed term, then revert.
variable_fixed.why: It decides whether your repayment is a known quantity or a moving one.

take_home_pay.plain: What actually lands in your account
take_home_pay.handover: This is your take-home pay, or net pay.
take_home_pay.glossary: What reaches you after tax and anything else taken out before you see it.
take_home_pay.why: It's the only income figure that tells you what you can actually spend.

marginal_rate.plain: The rate the next dollar you earn gets taxed at
marginal_rate.handover: Accountants call this your marginal rate.
marginal_rate.glossary: The tax rate that applies to your next dollar of income, rather than an average across everything you earn.
marginal_rate.why: Interest you earn is taxed at it. Interest an offset saves you isn't taxed at all. It's why the two aren't comparable on their headline rates.

consolidating.handover: Funds and planners call this consolidating.
consolidating.glossary: Closing super accounts and moving the balances into one.
consolidating.why: Each account carries its own fees, and closing one can close the insurance held inside it.

income_protection.plain: Cover that replaces part of your pay while you can't work
income_protection.glossary: Pays a monthly amount while you're unable to work, and stops when you return. Different from cover that pays a lump sum.
income_protection.why: It's the cover most households don't hold and the one that matches how their life is actually funded.

tpd.plain: Cover that pays if you could never work again
tpd.handover: Insurers call this TPD, for total and permanent disability.
tpd.glossary: A lump sum paid if you're permanently unable to work. A separate event from dying, and separate again from being off work for a while.
tpd.why: Holding one of the three doesn't cover you for the others.

waiting_period.plain: How long before a policy starts paying
waiting_period.glossary: The stretch between when you stop working and when a policy begins paying. Often 30, 60 or 90 days.
waiting_period.why: It's the gap your own money has to cover, which is what ties cover to your safety net.

binding_nomination.handover: The form that decides it is called a binding nomination.
binding_nomination.glossary: An instruction on your super account naming who receives it. Binding means the fund must follow it. Most expire after three years unless the fund offers a non-lapsing one.
binding_nomination.why: Your super usually isn't covered by your will. Without a valid nomination the fund's trustee decides.

enduring_poa.plain: Someone who can act for you if you can't
enduring_poa.handover: The document is an enduring power of attorney.
enduring_poa.glossary: Names a person to make decisions for you while you're alive but unable to make them yourself. A will only takes effect after death and doesn't cover this.
enduring_poa.why: It's the gap most households don't know they have.

deductible.plain: An expense you can claim against income
deductible.glossary: A cost you're allowed to subtract from income before tax is worked out.
deductible.why: Interest on an investment loan generally is. Interest on the loan for the home you live in isn't. It's why two identical-looking loans behave differently.

payg_instalments.plain: Paying tax through the year rather than in one hit
payg_instalments.handover: The ATO calls these PAYG instalments.
payg_instalments.glossary: Quarterly prepayments toward the tax on income no employer withholds for you.
payg_instalments.why: The year they start, it's common to pay last year's bill and this year's instalments across the same few months.
